paragraphs: This paper studies how to publish running totals while protecting each individual contribution. The input is a sequence of binary values, and each released estimate summarizes everything observed so far. Repeated releases require carefully designed noise: privacy must hold across the evolving sequence of outputs. A generalized version of this problem also appears in methods for private stochastic gradient descent.

The authors propose a simple alternative to the established binary mechanism. Their method takes constant time on average to generate each noise value, reduces noise variance by about a factor of four relative to that mechanism, and gives every time step the same noise distribution. These properties address both computational cost and uneven accuracy over time.

The paper also reports a practical runtime advantage. A straightforward Python implementation outperforms a recent alternative and an attempted acceleration of that alternative using specialized matrix multiplication. The contribution combines improved noise behavior with efficient generation, making the continual release procedure more practical.
neurips-2023-a-smooth-binary-mechanism-f.tldr: A simple private running-total mechanism reduces noise variance, keeps its distribution uniform over time, and generates noise efficiently.

paragraphs: The paper considers covariance estimation when fewer than half the observed points come from the Gaussian distribution of interest. That minority is assumed to consist of independent samples from an unknown Gaussian. The goal is to produce a short list of candidate covariance matrices, with a guarantee that at least one candidate approximates the desired covariance.

The authors give an algorithm whose sample requirements and running time are polynomial in the dimension and the inverse of the Gaussian sample fraction. Its list size grows proportionally to that inverse fraction, and its relative Frobenius error is bounded by a polynomial in the same quantity. The method uses spectral techniques and introduces a new multi-filtering procedure.

The result also supplies a spectral algorithm for robust partial clustering of Gaussian mixtures. Combined with other existing components, it yields a robust Gaussian-mixture learning algorithm that avoids Sum-of-Squares methods. This consequence resolves the stated open problem; the authors additionally suggest that their filtering approach may prove useful elsewhere.
neurips-2023-a-spectral-algorithm-for-li.tldr: A spectral algorithm estimates Gaussian covariance from a minority of valid samples by returning a short list containing a provably accurate candidate.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions when evaluating a function is expensive and only a limited number of evaluations are available. For structured or discrete objects, generative models can provide a latent space in which to search. However, searching that representation introduces a mismatch with the original optimization problem, potentially leading to suboptimal solutions.

CoBO addresses this mismatch by learning a latent space whose distances strongly correlate with differences in objective values. The aim is to make the geometry used by the optimizer more informative about the quantity it actually wants to improve. The method combines Lipschitz regularization, loss weighting, and trust region recoordination, concentrating on reducing the gap around promising regions.

The authors evaluate the approach on discrete optimization tasks, including molecule design and arithmetic expression fitting, and report high performance with a small evaluation budget. These findings support learning representations specifically for optimization: a useful search space should reflect the objective, as well as represent the candidate objects.
neurips-2023-advancing-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: CoBO improves latent-space Bayesian optimization by learning distances that better reflect differences in objective values.

paragraphs: Human preferences can disagree even when people judge the same language output. This creates a challenge for systems that learn a reward model from feedback and then optimize generated text against it. Collapsing judgments through majority voting or averaging can hide the extent of disagreement and produce a preference signal that mainly reflects a subset of people.

The paper proposes d-PM, a Bayesian preference model that accounts for the distribution of disagreement during training. This makes variation across human judgments part of the modeling problem. The authors then use scores from d-PM to train the language generation model through contrastive learning, addressing the complexity and inefficiency they associate with reinforcement learning training.

Experiments cover emotional support conversations and the generation of integrity-related rules of thumb. The method consistently exceeds previous state-of-the-art models in both automatic measures and human evaluations on these tasks. The findings support preserving information about disagreement when constructing the preference signal used to guide generation.
neurips-2023-aligning-language-models-wi.tldr: A Bayesian preference model captures human disagreement and supplies scores for contrastive training that improves results on two language generation tasks.

paragraphs: CLIP connects images and text, but its training cost can make experimentation difficult. This paper reports an inverse relationship between encoder size and the token sequence lengths that can be used during training: larger image and text encoders can be trained with shorter sequences. The particular strategy used to shorten those sequences substantially affects the quality of this relationship.

The authors use this finding to train CLIP with limited computational resources. On eight A100 GPUs, they report zero-shot ImageNet-1k top-1 accuracies of 63.2%, 67.8%, and 69.3% after approximately two, three, and four days, respectively. These examples demonstrate useful accuracy at several training durations under the stated hardware budget.

The approach also scales to a larger G/14 configuration, where the paper reports 83.0% zero-shot ImageNet-1k accuracy and roughly 33-fold faster training than its OpenCLIP counterpart. The central implication is that encoder size and token length should be considered together when seeking more computationally accessible image–text model training.
neurips-2023-an-inverse-scaling-law-for-.tldr: Larger CLIP encoders can train with shorter token sequences, enabling substantial computational savings with carefully chosen token reduction strategies.

paragraphs: Diff-Foley generates sound for silent video, a task with practical uses in film and video production. Successful output needs to fit both what appears on screen and when the visible events occur. The paper targets shortcomings in earlier video-to-audio methods concerning temporal synchronization and the relevance of generated sound to visual content.

The method first uses contrastive audio-visual pretraining to learn features aligned in timing and meaning. These visual features then condition a latent diffusion model operating in a representation of audio spectrograms. A cross-attention module lets generation use the aligned visual information to capture subtler relationships between the two modalities. An additional technique called double guidance further improves sample quality.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on the large-scale video-to-audio dataset used in their evaluation. They also demonstrate customized downstream fine-tuning to show practical applicability and adaptability. The findings support combining explicit audio-visual alignment with diffusion-based generation to improve both sound quality and its correspondence with video.
neurips-2023-diff-foley-synchronized-vid.tldr: Diff-Foley combines aligned audio-visual features with latent diffusion to generate higher-quality sound that better matches a silent video's content and timing.

paragraphs: Training a detector for three-dimensional scenes requires bounding box annotations that are difficult to obtain at scale. Semi-supervised methods supplement labeled data with unlabeled point clouds, often using a teacher model to generate pseudo-labels for a student. Their usefulness depends on producing reliable labels across diverse three-dimensional scenes, which remains challenging.

Diffusion-SS3D introduces a diffusion model to improve those pseudo-labels. The method adds noise to distributions describing object sizes and class labels, then uses denoising to produce bounding box outputs. It incorporates this process into the teacher–student framework so that the denoised boxes improve pseudo-label generation and contribute to the broader semi-supervised training process.

Experiments on ScanNet and SUN RGB-D report state-of-the-art performance compared with existing methods. The authors also analyze how diffusion design choices affect semi-supervised learning performance. The contribution places diffusion inside the labeling process: its generated outputs become supervision that helps a detector learn from point clouds without manually supplied boxes.
neurips-2023-diffusion-ss3d-diffusion-mo.tldr: Diffusion-SS3D uses denoising to improve pseudo-label bounding boxes and strengthen semi-supervised 3D object detection.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe models through continuous evolution, giving them a notion of continuous depth. This paper studies generalization for a broad family of parameterized differential equations whose parameters vary continuously with time. The family includes time-dependent neural ODEs, so the analysis addresses models whose transformations can change along the continuous trajectory.

The authors derive a generalization bound using a Lipschitz-based argument. Such a bound connects the mathematical properties of the model class to its ability to perform beyond the data used for learning. They then use the relationship between neural ODEs and deep residual networks to obtain a corresponding bound for a class of residual networks.

A notable feature of the residual-network bound is its dependence on the size of differences between consecutive weight matrices. This puts variation across successive layers directly into the generalization analysis. Numerical illustrations explore how that quantity affects generalization, connecting the theoretical result to observed network behavior within the studied setting.
neurips-2023-generalization-bounds-for-n.tldr: Generalization bounds connect continuous-time neural models and residual networks, highlighting the role of changes between successive weight matrices.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning trains models across devices without requiring a central server. A practical difficulty is that devices may hold data from substantially different distributions. This heterogeneity can degrade the resulting model's performance, making it important to design learning procedures that remain effective when local datasets differ.

Global Update Tracking, or GUT, is a tracking-based algorithm designed to reduce this sensitivity. The method aims to mitigate the effect of heterogeneous data without adding communication overhead. That combination matters because the proposed improvement addresses the learning behavior while preserving the communication requirements, an important consideration for training across a distributed network of devices.

The authors evaluate GUT across multiple architectures, network topologies, and vision datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and ImageNette. They report state-of-the-art results for decentralized learning with heterogeneous data, with test accuracy improvements of 1–6% over existing techniques. These are experimental findings across the tested configurations, supporting tracking as a useful approach to this distribution mismatch.
neurips-2023-global-update-tracking-a-de.tldr: GUT uses update tracking to improve decentralized learning on heterogeneous data without additional communication overhead.

paragraphs: Stein thinning post-processes samples produced by Markov chain Monte Carlo to obtain an approximation of a target distribution. It greedily reduces kernelized Stein discrepancy, a criterion requiring only the gradient of the target's log density. This makes the method suitable for Bayesian inference, where the paper highlights its potential to remove burn-in automatically and correct sampling bias.

Despite those advantages and its asymptotic convergence properties, Stein thinning can exhibit practical failure patterns that produce poor approximations. The authors analyze these pathologies theoretically to identify the mechanisms responsible. This distinction matters because a method's long-run guarantees can coexist with problematic behavior in the samples actually selected for use.

The paper then introduces regularized Stein thinning to alleviate the identified problems. The proposed modification is supported by theoretical guarantees and extensive experiments demonstrating its efficiency. The contribution connects an explanation of observed failures to a practical algorithmic adjustment, strengthening the use of discrepancy-based selection for MCMC post-processing.
neurips-2023-kernel-stein-discrepancy-th.tldr: The paper explains practical failure patterns in Stein thinning and introduces regularization to alleviate them.

paragraphs: Understanding a Transformer's learned algorithm by inspecting weights and activations can require considerable manual work. Such analysis can also fall short of a complete, faithful account of its computation. This paper instead designs Transformers so that training can produce models that are automatically convertible into readable programs.

The approach builds on RASP, a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. The authors develop a modified Transformer that supports gradient-based training and subsequent conversion into a discrete program. They call the resulting models Transformer Programs. Converting them into Python also makes established code analysis tools available for examining their behavior.

The authors test these models on in-context learning, algorithmic problems such as sorting and recognizing Dyck languages, and language tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. They find reasonable solutions with performance comparable to standard Transformers of similar size. The converted programs enable debugging of errors and identification of computational circuits for subproblems, demonstrating practical interpretability within the proposed model design.
neurips-2023-learning-transformer-progra.tldr: Modified Transformers can be trained with gradients and automatically converted into readable programs that support debugging and algorithm analysis.

paragraphs: Diffusion probabilistic models generate data through a reverse process that counteracts a forward corruption process. The reverse process relies on time-dependent data scores describing the evolving distribution. This paper examines a mathematical property of those scores and uses it to develop a calibration method for pretrained diffusion models.

The authors observe that the stochastic reverse process of data scores is a martingale. This property enables concentration bounds and an optional stopping theorem for the scores. From that analysis, they derive a simple calibration procedure that can reduce the score matching loss and consequently increase lower bounds on model likelihood.

The paper provides calibration guidance for different model parameterizations and describes the method as applicable to an arbitrary pretrained diffusion probabilistic model. Calibration is performed once, after which the resulting model can be reused for sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets empirically validate the proposal, connecting the theoretical score behavior to a practical adjustment of an already trained generator.
neurips-2023-on-calibrating-diffusion-pr.tldr: A martingale property of diffusion scores motivates a one-time calibration that can lower score matching loss and improve likelihood lower bounds.

paragraphs: Online experiments compare treatments to estimate their effects, but the way treatments are assigned influences how much information an experiment provides. This paper studies that design problem when assignments occur sequentially over time. Its objective is to make treatment effect estimates more precise by choosing how experimental observations are collected.

The authors propose three optimal allocation strategies for dynamic settings. These target the variance of the treatment effect estimator under non-Markov decision processes or Markov decision processes, including time-varying ones. They also develop estimation procedures using existing off-policy evaluation methods, linking the choice of treatment allocation to the subsequent estimation of effects.

The paper proves optimality of the proposed allocation design within the studied setting and establishes upper bounds on the estimators' mean squared errors. Experiments in various environments demonstrate the methods' effectiveness. Together, the results treat experimental design and policy evaluation as connected problems: the sequence of treatment assignments is chosen to support more informative comparisons.
neurips-2023-optimal-treatment-allocatio.tldr: Three sequential treatment allocation strategies aim to minimize estimation variance, with optimality proofs and error bounds in the studied decision-process settings.

paragraphs: An inverse problem starts with observations and tries to recover the underlying signal that produced them. When the physical relationship is nonlinear, solving this problem can require costly repeated linearizations and inversions. PETAL replaces the original forward calculation with a learned emulator and uses automatic differentiation within classical optimization to recover the input.

The emulator explicitly incorporates known physics. It contains linearizations of the forward model around multiple reference points and learns how to combine them through a weighted average. This design gives the learned model access to information about the physical system that a purely supervised black-box emulator would otherwise leave unused.

The authors report that these physics-based linearizations improve forward prediction and provide richer gradient information during inversion, leading to more accurate signal recovery. They demonstrate the approach in simulated ocean acoustic tomography for the Gulf of Mexico, recovering variations in ocean sound speed profiles from acoustic observations. This example illustrates how incorporating physical approximations can help both prediction and reconstruction.
neurips-2023-petal-physics-emulation-thr.tldr: PETAL combines learned weights with physical linearizations to build an emulator that improves signal recovery in an ocean acoustic tomography simulation.

paragraphs: Predicting how an amino acid mutation changes protein–protein binding is useful for protein engineering and therapeutic discovery. A major obstacle is the limited supply of experimental binding energy annotations for training computational models. SidechainDiff addresses this shortage by learning representations from experimental protein structures that do not require those annotations.

The method uses a Riemannian diffusion model to learn how protein side-chain conformations are generated. The learned model also supplies representations of the structural context around mutations at protein–protein interfaces. This connects structural generation with prediction: information learned about side-chain configurations becomes an input for estimating a mutation's effect on binding.

Using those representations, the authors report state-of-the-art performance on binding-effect prediction. They also present SidechainDiff as the first diffusion-based generative model focused on side chains, extending a line of work that had mainly targeted protein backbones. The contribution demonstrates how learning from unlabeled structures can support a prediction task constrained by scarce experimental outcome labels.
neurips-2023-predicting-mutational-effec.tldr: SidechainDiff learns side-chain structural representations from unlabeled protein structures to improve predictions of mutation effects on protein binding.

paragraphs: Privacy auditing examines what a trained learning system reveals about its training data. Standard auditing methods can be expensive because they require training many models. This paper proposes an auditing scheme that obtains useful evidence from a single training run, reducing the repeated training needed to evaluate a differentially private machine learning system.

The method exploits the ability to add or remove multiple training examples independently. This creates parallel opportunities for an audit within one run. Its analysis uses the relationship between differential privacy and statistical generalization, avoiding the cost associated with a group-privacy analysis. The scheme requires minimal assumptions about the learning algorithm and supports both black-box and white-box access.

Applied to differentially private stochastic gradient descent, the framework produces meaningful empirical lower bounds on privacy loss after training only one model. The authors contrast this with standard approaches requiring hundreds of models. These lower bounds provide evidence about privacy loss; their value here is that the evidence becomes substantially cheaper to obtain.
neurips-2023-privacy-auditing-with-one-1.tldr: A privacy auditing scheme uses independently varied training examples to obtain meaningful empirical privacy lower bounds from one training run.

paragraphs: Text models can be vulnerable to small changes in their inputs. This paper investigates attacks that alter a single punctuation mark, aiming to disrupt model behavior while minimally affecting how people perceive and understand the text. The considered edits include inserting, moving, deleting, and replacing punctuation.

The authors also introduce Text Position Punctuation Embedding and Paraphrase, or TPPEP, to find a useful attack position without exhaustively checking every possibility. They provide a mathematical interpretation of this search method. Its integrated Text Position Punctuation Embedding component enables the punctuation attack to be applied at constant time cost, according to the paper.

Experiments on public datasets and state-of-the-art models show promising fooling rates and support the effectiveness of the proposed position embedding. Additional applications to summarization, semantic similarity scoring, and text-to-image tasks yield encouraging results. The findings highlight a mismatch between human and model sensitivity: a punctuation edit with little perceived effect can still substantially alter a model's behavior.
neurips-2023-punctuation-level-attack-si.tldr: Single-punctuation edits can fool text models, and a proposed search method finds attack positions without exhaustive evaluation.

paragraphs: An ordered top-K adversarial attack aims to make a classifier rank multiple target classes in a specified order. This imposes more control over the output than changing only the highest-ranked prediction. QuadAttacK studies these targeted attacks in a clear-box setting and seeks to construct them at low computational cost.

The method solves a quadratic program in the feature space immediately before the final linear classifier. It directly enforces the attack constraint there, using the class-related organization of that representation. After finding a feature perturbation, it uses a single backpropagation step to compute a corresponding perturbation of the input data.

The authors evaluate the method on ImageNet-1k using ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, ViT-B, and DEiT-S. Under the reported small budget, successful ordered attacks extend from K=10 to K=20. The method also improves success rates for K=5 across all tested models while retaining performance at K=1. These findings demonstrate stronger control over class rankings in the evaluated clear-box setting.
neurips-2023-quadattac-k-a-quadratic-pro.tldr: QuadAttacK solves a quadratic program in feature space to construct efficient attacks that impose a chosen ordering on multiple predicted classes.

paragraphs: RealTime QA evaluates whether question-answering systems can respond to events and information that have just become relevant. The platform releases questions and evaluates systems regularly, weekly in the version described. This makes changing world knowledge part of the benchmark and tests the ability to answer questions whose information needs arise after a model's pretraining.

The authors build baseline systems using pretrained language models, including GPT-3 and T5, and present a year of real-time evaluation results. Their experiments show that GPT-3 can often update its generated answers when supplied with newly retrieved documents. This finding highlights current information retrieval as an important component of timely question answering.

A significant failure pattern appears when the retrieved documents lack enough information: GPT-3 tends to fall back on outdated answers. The authors identify recognizing these unanswerable cases as a research direction, potentially involving communication with the user or changes to retrieval. The benchmark exposes both the benefit of fresh evidence and the challenge of recognizing when it is insufficient.
neurips-2023-realtime-qa-what-s-the-answ.tldr: RealTime QA tests answers to current events and shows that fresh retrieval often helps, while insufficient evidence can leave models producing outdated answers.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback learns a reward signal from people's preferences, reducing the need to hand-design rewards. SeqRank seeks to make that feedback more productive by organizing comparisons into a sequential ranking of trajectories. This structure allows additional preference queries to be derived from the collected ranking information.

Each comparison pairs a defender from previously selected trajectories with a challenger from the remaining replay buffer. One strategy chooses the most recently selected trajectory as defender; another chooses the most preferred trajectory so far. The paper also examines reward-model empirical risk convergence and generalization using Rademacher complexity, addressing the dependence created by reusing comparison information.

The reported average feedback efficiency is at least 39.2% higher than the baseline. Both strategies outperform conventional pairwise comparison, while the preferred-defender strategy improves average locomotion reward and manipulation success rate by 29.0% and 25.0%, respectively. The results support structured reuse of human comparisons while accounting for the relationship between feedback efficiency and data dependency.
neurips-2023-sequential-preference-ranki.tldr: SeqRank organizes sequential trajectory comparisons into preference rankings to extract more learning value from human feedback.

paragraphs: The paper treats optimizer discovery as a search over programs. Efficient search explores an infinite, sparse space of possible algorithms, while program selection and simplification address the gap between inexpensive proxy tasks and intended target tasks. This process discovers Lion, a compact optimizer for neural network training.

Lion stores only momentum, making it more memory-efficient than Adam. It uses the sign of an update to give every parameter update the same magnitude. The authors report gains across image classification, vision–language learning, and diffusion modeling, including up to fivefold savings in image pretraining compute and up to 2.3-fold savings for diffusion training. Language-modeling and fine-tuning results are similar to or better than Adam's.

The benefits depend on the setting. Reported gains grow with training batch size, and Lion requires a smaller learning rate than Adam because its sign-based update has a larger norm. The authors also identify cases with small or statistically insignificant improvements. The contribution combines a program-search discovery method with an optimizer whose practical advantages vary across workloads.
neurips-2023-symbolic-discovery-of-optim.tldr: Program search discovers Lion, a memory-efficient sign-based optimizer with strong results across several tasks and gains that depend on the training setting.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning is widely used in reinforcement learning, but understanding when it converges remains important. This paper studies the algorithm through an optimization viewpoint. It interprets TD as an iterative procedure in which the function being minimized changes at each step, making the evolution of that objective part of the convergence problem.

The authors examine a classical example where TD diverges and identify two forces that govern whether its behavior converges or diverges. They formalize this account for linear TD with quadratic loss and prove that convergence depends on the interaction between those forces. This turns an analysis of failure into a framework for explaining the algorithm's behavior.

The paper then extends the optimization perspective to establish convergence beyond linear approximation and squared loss. Its contribution is a broader theoretical explanation for TD's successful use in reinforcement learning. The results explain convergence within the settings analyzed, with the changing objective and the balance of the identified forces central to the argument.
neurips-2023-td-convergence-an-optimizat.tldr: Viewing TD as optimization of a changing objective yields convergence results governed by the interaction of two identified forces.

paragraphs: Estimating camera motion becomes difficult when the scene itself deforms. Many existing methods rely on some static scene content to anchor their estimates, but that assumption can fail in applications such as endoscopy. The paper addresses both this tracking challenge and the shortage of suitable quantitative evaluation data for exploratory camera trajectories.

The Drunkard's Dataset provides synthetic trajectories through three-dimensional building scenes in which every surface undergoes non-rigid deformation. Simulation supplies ground-truth camera poses alongside high-resolution color images, depth, optical flow, and surface normals. The authors describe it as the first large collection combining exploratory trajectories, fully deforming surfaces, and ground-truth information.

The accompanying Drunkard's Odometry method separates estimated optical flow into rigid camera motion and non-rigid scene deformation. The paper evaluates several baselines to validate the dataset and introduces a tracking error metric that does not require ground truth. Together, the dataset, method, and metric provide resources for studying navigation when a static visual reference is unavailable.
neurips-2023-the-drunkards-odometry-esti.tldr: The paper introduces a fully deforming synthetic scene benchmark and an odometry method that separates camera motion from scene deformation.

paragraphs: Irregular time series contain observations taken at uneven intervals and can be highly sparse, particularly in healthcare. Specialized models try to handle these patterns directly, but their dynamics remain challenging. This paper takes a visual approach: it converts the measurements into line graph images and treats the resulting prediction problem as image classification.

The method applies pretrained vision transformers to those graphs. This reduces the need for specialized algorithm designs for irregular sampling and creates a way to use pretrained image models for time series classification. The authors suggest that this perspective could potentially support a universal time series modeling framework, while their demonstrated application focuses on classification.

Experiments on healthcare and human activity datasets outperform leading specialized methods. The approach is also robust in leave-sensors-out tests, where variables are absent at evaluation time. With half the variables masked, the paper reports an absolute improvement of 42.8 F1 score points over leading specialized baselines, demonstrating strong performance under that missing-observation setting.
neurips-2023-time-series-as-images-visio.tldr: Turning irregular time series into graph images lets pretrained vision transformers deliver strong classification results, including when many variables are missing.

paragraphs: Four-bit arithmetic offers a route to faster neural network training, but earlier approaches relied on custom number formats unsupported by contemporary hardware. This paper develops a Transformer training method in which every matrix multiplication uses INT4 arithmetic. Achieving useful accuracy at that precision requires handling the different numerical structures of activations and gradients.

For the forward pass, the authors identify outliers as a key problem and introduce a Hadamard quantizer to suppress them. For backpropagation, they exploit structural sparsity in gradients using bit splitting and leverage score sampling. These dedicated quantization techniques address the distinct difficulties of the two stages of training.

The method achieves competitive accuracy across natural language understanding, machine translation, and image classification, and can run on the GPU generation considered in the paper. Its prototype linear operator is up to 2.2 times faster than FP16 counterparts. For sufficiently large models, average training acceleration is 17.8%, showing that the larger operator-level speedup translates into a more modest overall gain.
neurips-2023-training-transformers-with-.tldr: Specialized activation and gradient quantizers enable INT4 Transformer matrix multiplications, delivering competitive accuracy and faster training for sufficiently large models.
